m1-s1.title: Declare a FastAPI application instance named 'app'.
m1-s1.summary: Import the FastAPI class and create an app instance to start building your API.
you_will_learn: Import FastAPI from the fastapi package
Instantiate the FastAPI class as a variable
Understand that app is an instance of FastAPI

blocks.heading: Creating Your FastAPI App
blocks.body: To start building your API, you must first import the `FastAPI` class from the `fastapi` package. Then, instantiate this class and assign it to a variable, typically named `app`. This `app` variable is an instance of the `FastAPI` class and serves as the main point of interaction for creating all your API endpoints.

items.title: Importing FastAPI
items.text: Use `from fastapi import FastAPI` to bring the class into your current Python file.

items.title: Instantiating the App
items.text: Call `FastAPI()` with no arguments and assign the result to a variable like `app`.

items.title: The App Instance
items.text: The `app` variable is now an instance of the `FastAPI` class, ready for decorators.

blocks.title: Basic FastAPI Setup

blocks.text: Always define `app` before adding route handlers like `@app.get`. The order matters for the code to work correctly.

m1-s2.title: Define a path operation decorator for a GET request at the root path.
m1-s2.summary: Learn how to use the @app.get decorator to define a GET route at the root path.
you_will_learn: Add a GET route using @app.get
Specify the path in parentheses
Define the handler function below

blocks.heading: Defining a GET Route
blocks.body: To handle GET requests, use the `@app.get` decorator. Place it directly above your function definition. The path (e.g., `/`) goes inside the parentheses. FastAPI will automatically link this function to the specified URL and HTTP method.

items.title: Decorator Syntax
items.text: Use `@app.get("/path")` to register a handler for GET requests at that specific path.

items.title: Function Placement
items.text: The function definition must immediately follow the decorator line without interruption.

blocks.title: Root GET Endpoint

blocks.text: You can use other methods like `@app.post`, `@app.put`, or `@app.delete` for different HTTP verbs.

blocks.heading: Define an Async Function Returning JSON
blocks.body: To make a function asynchronous, use the `async` keyword before `def`. To return data as JSON, simply return a Python dictionary. FastAPI automatically converts this dictionary into a JSON response for the client.

items.title: The Async Keyword
items.text: Place `async` immediately before `def` to define an asynchronous function.

items.title: Return a Dictionary
items.text: Returning a standard Python dict allows FastAPI to serialize it directly to JSON.

items.title: Automatic Conversion
items.text: FastAPI handles the conversion of your returned dictionary into the HTTP response body automatically.

blocks.title: Async Function with Dict Return

blocks.text: You can also use a normal `def` without `async`, but using `async` is standard for modern async operations.

m2-s1.title: Define a FastAPI route that accepts a path parameter with a specific Python type annotation and returns that value in the JSON response.
m2-s1.summary: Declare path parameter types and see FastAPI convert strings to integers automatically.
you_will_learn: Add type annotations to function arguments
Receive converted integer values in your code
Understand automatic parsing from URL paths

blocks.heading: Path Parameter Types and Conversion
blocks.body: Declare the expected Python type for a path parameter directly in the function signature using standard annotations. When FastAPI receives a request, it automatically converts the string from the URL path into the declared type before passing it to your function.

items.title: Type Annotations
items.text: Add a Python type like `int` or `str` after the parameter name in the function definition.

items.title: Automatic Conversion
items.text: FastAPI converts the URL string to the declared type, so your function receives an integer, not a string.

items.title: Validation Errors
items.text: If the URL value cannot be converted to the declared type, FastAPI returns a validation error instead of crashing.

blocks.title: Integer Path Parameter

blocks.text: If you omit the type annotation, FastAPI treats the value as a string. Adding `int` enables automatic conversion and validation.

exercise.title: Echo an integer path parameter

exercise.explanation: The int annotation tells FastAPI to convert the path string to an integer. Valid integers return 200 with the converted value, while non-integers like 'abc' or floats like '3.14' trigger a 422 validation error.

blocks.heading: Creating an Enum Subclass for Path Parameters
blocks.body: To restrict valid values for a path parameter, create a custom Enum class that inherits from both `str` and `Enum`. Import `Enum` from the standard library. Define your class with fixed attributes representing valid strings. Inheriting from `str` tells FastAPI the parameter expects a string type, ensuring correct API documentation rendering and validation.

items.title: Inherit from str
items.text: The Enum must inherit from `str` so FastAPI knows to validate incoming path values as strings.

items.title: Define fixed values
items.text: Set class attributes with string literals to define the only allowed values for that parameter.

items.title: Use in type annotation
items.text: Apply the new Enum class as the type hint for your path parameter argument.

blocks.title: Defining a ModelName Enum

blocks.text: Access the underlying string value using `.value` (e.g., `model_name.value`) or compare directly with the member (e.g., `model_name is ModelName.alexnet`).

m2-s3.title: Implement logic within a route handler to return different messages based on which predefined Enum value was passed in the path.
m2-s3.summary: Use Enum comparisons to handle specific model names and rely on FastAPI validation for invalid inputs.
you_will_learn: Compare an Enum instance using the 'is' operator
Access the underlying string value with .value

blocks.heading: Comparing and Validating Enum Path Parameters
blocks.body: To check which specific model was requested, compare the incoming `model_name` instance directly to the class attributes using the `is` operator (e.g., `if model_name is ModelName.alexnet`). You can also access the raw string value via `.value`. FastAPI automatically validates path parameters against the Enum definition; if a client sends an invalid value, FastAPI returns a 422 error response.

items.title: Use 'is' for Comparison
items.text: Compare the parameter instance to class attributes like `ModelName.alexnet` using the `is` operator to match specific members.

items.title: Access Raw Values
items.text: Retrieve the underlying string data by accessing the `.value` attribute of the Enum member inside your handler function.

items.title: Automatic Validation
items.text: FastAPI rejects any path parameter value that does not match a defined Enum member and returns a 422 error automatically.

blocks.title: Handling Model Requests with Enums

blocks.text: Remember that FastAPI converts the Enum member to its string value before sending it back in the JSON response.

m3-s1.title: Define a FastAPI endpoint that accepts optional query parameters with default values and returns different responses based on their presence.

you_will_learn: Declare optional parameters with None defaults
Use Annotated for validation on optional params
Return different JSON based on parameter presence

blocks.heading: Optional Query Parameters
blocks.body: To make a query parameter optional, set its default value to `None`. FastAPI automatically detects this and treats the parameter as not required. You can also use `Annotated` with `Query` for validation rules like minimum length while keeping it optional.

items.title: Set Default to None
items.text: Declare an optional parameter by assigning `None` as the default value, e.g., `q: str | None = None`.

items.title: Use Annotated for Validation
items.text: Combine `Annotated` with `Query(min_length=3)` to add validation rules while keeping the parameter optional.

items.title: Check Parameter Presence
items.text: Inside your function, check if the parameter is not `None` to decide whether to include it in the response.

blocks.title: Optional Query with Default

blocks.text: FastAPI knows a parameter is optional because of the default value `= None`, not just the type annotation.

docs.label: `Query` as the default value or in `Annotated`
Query parameter list / multiple values with defaults

m3-s2.title: Declare a query parameter with a boolean type that automatically converts string inputs to boolean values.

you_will_learn: Use bool type for query params
Understand automatic string-to-bool conversion

blocks.heading: Boolean Query Parameters
blocks.body: Declare a parameter with type `bool`. FastAPI automatically converts common truthy strings like 'true', '1', or 'on' to Python `True`, and falsy strings like 'false', '0', or 'off' to `False`. If the parameter is omitted from the URL, FastAPI uses the default value you specify.

items.title: Default Value
items.text: If a boolean query parameter has no explicit default, FastAPI defaults it to `False`.

items.title: Truthy Strings
items.text: Strings like 'true', '1', 'on', or 'yes' are automatically converted to Python `True`.

blocks.title: Boolean Query Parameter Example

blocks.text: An empty value like ?short= or an unrecognized value like ?short=maybe will produce a 422 validation error.

docs.label: `Query` as the default value or in `Annotated`

m3-s3.title: Create a Pydantic model class that inherits from BaseModel with required and optional fields.
m3-s3.summary: Import BaseModel from Pydantic and define optional fields using type unions.
you_will_learn: Import BaseModel from pydantic
Create a class inheriting from BaseModel
Make fields optional with None defaults
Use union syntax for optional types

blocks.heading: Creating Pydantic Models with Optional Fields
blocks.body: To create a model, import `BaseModel` from the `pydantic` package. Define a class that inherits from `BaseModel`. To make a field optional, set its default value to `None`. In Python 3.10+, use the union syntax `Type | None` to indicate an attribute can be either the specified type or `None`.

items.title: Import BaseModel
items.text: Use `from pydantic import BaseModel` to access the base class for your models.

items.title: Optional Fields Syntax
items.text: Declare optional fields by setting a default value of `None` and using `Type | None` as the annotation.

items.title: Required vs Optional
items.text: Fields without a default value are required; fields with `default=None` are optional.

blocks.title: Defining an Item Model
blocks.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str | None = None
    price: float
    tax: float | None = None

@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item: Item):
    return item

blocks.text: Remember that `Field` is imported from `pydantic`, not `fastapi`. Use it to add extra metadata like validation rules or titles.

blocks.heading: Mixing Path Parameters and Request Bodies
blocks.body: To accept both path parameters and a request body, declare them as separate function arguments. FastAPI automatically distinguishes their sources: arguments matching the URL path pattern (like `{item_id}`) are taken from the path, while arguments typed as Pydantic models are taken from the request body.

items.title: Automatic Source Detection
items.text: FastAPI automatically routes path variables to the URL and Pydantic models to the JSON body without extra configuration.

blocks.text: Remember that a single HTTP request can only have one body. If you declare multiple Pydantic models in the function signature, FastAPI will combine them into one body.

m4-s1.title: Declare a Pydantic model with mixed Path, Query, and Body parameters using `Field` for validation.
m4-s1.summary: Learn to mix Path, Query, and Body parameters in one endpoint using Pydantic Field for validation.
you_will_learn: Import Field from pydantic
Add constraints like max_length or gt
Mix path query and body params

blocks.heading: Using Field for Model Validation
blocks.body: Import `Field` from `pydantic`, not `fastapi`. Use it inside Pydantic models to add metadata like titles, defaults, or constraints (e.g., `max_length`, `gt`). You can freely mix Path, Query, and Body parameters in a single endpoint. FastAPI automatically detects the source: path params use `{param}`, query uses singular types with defaults, and Pydantic models become request bodies.

items.title: Import Field Correctly
items.text: Always import `Field` from `pydantic`, not `fastapi`. It works like `Query` or `Body` but for model attributes.

items.title: Mix Parameter Types
items.text: You can combine path, query, and body parameters in one function. FastAPI knows where to get each value automatically.

items.title: Use Annotated with Body
items.text: Prefer `Annotated[Model, Body(embed=True)]` for clarity, though plain model types also work as request bodies.

blocks.title: Mixed Parameters with Field Validation

blocks.text: Remember that `Field` is from `pydantic`. Use it in models, while `Path`, `Query`, and `Body` are from `fastapi`.

you_will_learn: Declare a list of strings using square brackets
Define a set of unique items with the set type
Use a Pydantic model as an element inside a list
Understand how to handle nested JSON structures

blocks.heading: Declaring List and Set Attributes in Models
blocks.body: In FastAPI, you can define attributes that hold lists or sets of other types. Use square brackets `[]` for lists and the `set` keyword for sets. You can also nest Pydantic models inside these containers to handle complex JSON structures.

items.title: List Syntax
items.text: Use `list[Type]` to declare a list of specific items, like `tags: list[str] = []`.

items.title: Set Syntax
items.text: Use `set[Type]` for unique items, such as `tags: set[str] = set()`.

items.title: Nested Models
items.text: You can define a list of Pydantic models like `images: list[Image] | None = None`.

blocks.title: Model with List and Set Attributes
blocks.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class Image(BaseModel):
    url: str
    name: str

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float
    tags: set[str] = set()
    images: list[Image] | None = None

blocks.text: FastAPI automatically converts JSON arrays into Python lists or sets based on your type annotation.

docs.label: Declare a `list` with a type parameter

blocks.heading: Separate Input and Output Models
blocks.body: To filter sensitive data like passwords, define a `UserIn` model that includes the password field and a `UserOut` model that excludes it. Annotate your endpoint with `response_model=UserOut`. FastAPI will automatically convert the returned object to match the output model, effectively removing fields not declared in it.

items.title: Define Output Model
items.text: Create a Pydantic model that inherits from BaseModel but omits sensitive fields like passwords.

items.title: Annotate Endpoint
items.text: Pass the output model to the `response_model` parameter of your route decorator instead of the return type annotation.

items.title: Exclude Unset Values
items.text: Set `response_model_exclude_unset=True` to omit fields that were not explicitly set in the returned data.

blocks.title: Filtering Passwords from Response
blocks.code:
from typing import Any

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr

app = FastAPI()

class UserIn(BaseModel):
    username: str
    password: str
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str | None = None

class UserOut(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str | None = None

@app.post("/user/", response_model=UserOut)
async def create_user(user: UserIn) -> Any:
    return user

blocks.text: If you use `response_model_exclude_unset=True`, fields with default values or None will not appear in the JSON response.

m4-s4.title: Configure a response to return a Union of multiple types or an arbitrary dict with typed keys and values.
m4-s4.summary: Learn to declare FastAPI responses using Union types or arbitrary dicts with typed keys and values.
you_will_learn: Use typing.Union for multiple response types
Place specific types before general ones in Unions
Define dict[str, float] for typed dictionary responses

blocks.heading: Declaring Union or Dict Responses
blocks.body: To return a response that can be one of several types, use `typing.Union` with the specific type listed first. For an arbitrary dictionary where you know the key and value types (e.g., string keys with float values), declare the return type as `dict[str, float]`. FastAPI uses these annotations to validate data and generate documentation.

items.title: Union Syntax Order
items.text: Always list the most specific Pydantic model first in a Union, followed by less specific types like dict.

items.title: Typed Dict Keys
items.text: Use `dict[str, float]` to accept JSON keys as strings that are automatically converted to integers for float values.

blocks.title: Union and Typed Dict Response

blocks.text: Remember that JSON keys are always strings; Pydantic converts string keys like '1' to integers if your type expects `int`.

m5-s1.title: Raise an HTTPException with a specific status code and custom headers to return a structured error response.
m5-s1.summary: Learn to raise HTTPException with custom status codes and headers for structured error responses.
you_will_learn: Import HTTPException from FastAPI
Pass status_code argument when raising errors
Add custom headers to error responses
Use detail field for error messages

blocks.heading: Raising HTTPExceptions with Status Codes and Headers
blocks.body: To return a structured error, import `HTTPException` from `fastapi`. Raise it inside your endpoint logic when an error occurs. Pass the `status_code` integer (e.g., 404) to set the HTTP status. You can also pass a `headers` dictionary to add custom headers like `X-Error`. The `detail` field holds the message sent in the response body.

items.title: Importing HTTPException
items.text: Use `from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException` at the top of your file to access the exception class.

items.title: Setting Status Code
items.text: Pass an integer like `status_code=404` inside the `raise HTTPException(...)` call to define the response status.

items.title: Adding Custom Headers
items.text: Include a `headers` dictionary in the exception arguments to attach custom headers to the error response.

blocks.title: Raising an HTTPException with Headers

blocks.text: Remember to `raise` the exception, not `return` it. Returning will bypass FastAPI's automatic error handling and custom response formatting.

m5-s2.title: Define a dependency function that accepts query parameters and returns a dictionary of values.
m5-s2.summary: Learn to define dependency functions with query params using Annotated and Depends.
you_will_learn: Declare a dependency function accepting query parameters
Use Annotated to combine type hints with dependencies
Pass the dependency object without calling it directly

blocks.heading: Defining Dependencies with Query Parameters
blocks.body: Create an async function that accepts query parameters like `q`, `skip`, and `limit`. Return a dictionary from this function. In your endpoint, use `Annotated[dict, Depends(dependency_function)]` to tell FastAPI to call the dependency and inject its result into the parameter.

items.title: Dependency Function Structure
items.text: The dependency is a callable function that accepts query parameters and returns a value.

items.title: Using Annotated with Depends
items.text: Combine the return type hint with `Depends()` inside `Annotated` to define the parameter source.

items.title: Do Not Call the Dependency
items.text: Pass the function object directly to `Depends()`, do not add parentheses or call it manually.

blocks.title: Shared Dependency with Query Params
blocks.code:
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
    return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}

CommonsDep = Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: CommonsDep):
    return commons

blocks.text: FastAPI calls the dependency function automatically. Do not add parentheses when passing it to `Depends()`.

blocks.heading: Classes as Dependencies
blocks.body: A Python class is a "callable" because you can create an instance by calling it, like `Cat()`. FastAPI treats classes the same way as functions for dependencies. It analyzes the parameters defined in your class's `__init__` method.

items.title: Make Classes Callable
items.text: Define a class with an `__init__` method to accept arguments and store them as instance attributes.

items.title: Use Annotated for Dependencies
items.text: Wrap the class type in `Annotated` inside the endpoint function argument to tell FastAPI to call it.

items.title: Pass Dependency Objects
items.text: FastAPI calls your dependency class automatically; you receive the instance, not the class itself.

blocks.text: Prefer using `Annotated` with class dependencies over non-annotated versions for better tooling support.
